newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela severance pay reform worth price-Petkoff.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela severance pay reform worth price-Petkoff.

text.p: Venezuela's recent agreement to reform its severance payment system is one of the country's most important structural changes in recent years, and while it comes with a macroeconomic cost the price is worth paying, Planning Minister Teodoro Petkoff said.
"It may add a few points to this year's inflation ... but the 35 percent annual target is still a valid one," Petkoff told reporters after a seminar on the reform.

The severance pay reform bill is expected to be passed by Congress shortly after the Easter holidays, Petkoff said, although supporting legislation -- such as regulations governing pensions funds -- "will clearly take much longer."
As Venezuelan workers and employees grapple to understand the agreement signed four days ago, "it's natural that many people still have doubts and uncertainties," Petkoff said.
But essentially "for workers it's a system that ensures adequate compensation, while for businesses it eliminates retroactivity and uncertainty," he explained.
The agreement crucially removes a retroactivity clause which meant annual severance payments were calculated based on an employee's most recent wage, so impeding wage rises.

However, before moving onto the new system -- that will see workers be paid their severance pay annually into savings accounts -- employers must first pay-off old liabilities that have accumulated over the years.
"The rise in real wages this year from this will be very large," said leading business chamber Fedecamaras Vice President Aurelio Concheso.

Under the agreement, the private sector must meet 25 percent of its past severance liabilities within 180 days, while the public sector only 150,000 bolivars ($314) per worker. Total payments must be made within five years in both cases.
Petkoff said the public sector's total liability was around 3.5 trillion bolivars ($7.3 billion), but he skirted reporters' questions as to the fiscal impact of payments this year.
Venezuela's central administration employees some 800,000 workers, rising to 1.3 million if workers at state-owned industries are included.

New York based IDEA recently estimated the annual fiscal cost going forward will be $870 million. The total cost for this year will be some $1.12 billion, once the 150,000 bolivar per worker payment is included, IDEA forecast, equal to 6.9 percent of the total budget.
